text: Pico says he was moved to examine the secrets of the book of Moses by emulation of the studies of Lorenzo dei Medici, and dedicates the work to him.

quotes.text: Emulation of your studies, Lorenzo dei Medici, has moved me to examine the secrets of the book of Moses
These labors of mine, such as they are, the first efforts of my youth thus far, are offered to you, most illustrious Lorenzo

bears_on.note: Pico presents the Heptaplus as a gift to Lorenzo, whose leisure at Fiesole made it possible.

text: Pico says the work was written at Fiesole in a retreat provided by the man he addresses, made pleasanter by the constant visits of Angelo Poliziano.

quotes.text: because you provided me with the leisure of this very retreat at Fiesole in which they were born, a retreat frequently made more enjoyable by the visits, or rather the constant attendance, of your friend Angelo Poliziano

bears_on.note: Poliziano is described as a constant visitor during the writing of the Heptaplus.
Lorenzo supplied the retreat at Fiesole.

text: Pico believes that the secrets of all nature are contained in the works of the six days.

quotes.text: those celebrated works of the six days, in which there is great reason for us to believe that the secrets of all nature are contained

text: Pico argues that the sages of old either did not write on religious subjects or wrote of them under another guise, which is why such subjects are called mysteries.

quotes.text: it was a well-known practice of the sages of old either simply not to write on religious subjects or to write of them under some other guise. For this reason these subjects are called mysteries

judged.justification: Grounds the reading of the surface of Moses as a veil for a hidden philosophy.

text: Pico says Plato himself concealed his doctrines beneath allegory, myth, mathematical images and unintelligible signs.

quotes.text: Plato himself concealed his doctrines beneath coverings of allegory, veils of myth, mathematical images, and unintelligible signs of fugitive meaning.

text: Pico cites Dionysius the Areopagite, whom he calls Paul's disciple, as witness that the churches kept the more secret doctrines for oral communication to the initiated.

quotes.text: Paul's disciple Dionysius the Areopagite writes that it was a settled and holy custom in the churches not to communicate the more secret doctrines in writing but only by voice and to those who had been properly initiated.

judged.justification: Shows Pico treating Dionysius as a disciple of Paul who reports apostolic esoteric practice, the stance he takes in the Third Exposition.

text: Pico holds that if the book treats anywhere of the whole world, it does so above all where it treats of the emanation of all things from God and of the grade, number and order of the parts of the world.

quotes.text: if in any part of his work he buried the treasures of all true philosophy as in a field, he must have done so most of all in the part where avowedly and most loftily he philosophizes on the emanation of all things from God, and on the grade, number, and order of the parts of the world.

text: Pico says he will make no mention of what earlier interpreters wrote in the Chaldean language, and will offer seven interpretations of his own discovery.

quotes.text: We shall make no mention at present of what Ionethes or Anchelos or the venerable Simeon bequeathed in the Chaldean language
Going beyond all these, we shall suggest seven other interpretations of our own discovery and development

open_questions.text: The proem defers any use of the Hebrew authorities; how far the Heptaplus later draws on them is left for the reader to check against the text.

judged.justification: Pico says he sets aside the Chaldean and Hebrew commentators and claims the seven interpretations as his own invention.

text: Pico names three difficulties: keeping Moses from seeming to speak inadequately, keeping a single coherent line of interpretation, and avoiding making Moses say anything alien to nature or to the truths of the better philosophers.

quotes.text: The first is to keep Moses from seeming to have spoken inadequately or with too little learning and wisdom.
The second difficulty is to work out a self-consistent and coherent course of interpretation

The third difficulty is to avoid making the Prophet, or the Holy Spirit through the Prophet, assert anything strange or wonderful or alien to the nature of things as they are observed, or to the truths ascertained by the better philosophers

text: Pico says he will interpret the whole creation continuously and without confusion in seven senses, and not merely one, in a completely new work.

quotes.text: See how great a task we have conceived, which it may not be easy to carry out (May we be able to achieve it!), to interpret the entire creation of the world continuously and without confusion in not merely one but seven senses, without reference to earlier works, but producing a work completely new from the beginning!

text: Pico says antiquity imagined three worlds: the ultramundane, which theologians call the angelic and philosophers the intelligible, the celestial, and the sublunary world we inhabit.

quotes.text: Antiquity imagined three worlds. Highest of all is that ultramundane one which theologians call the angelic and philosophers the intelligible, and of which, Plato says in the Phaedrus, no one has worthily sung. Next to this comes the celestial world, and last of all, this sublunary one which we inhabit.

judged.justification: Fixes Pico's own equation of the angelic world with the philosophers' intelligible world.

text: Pico characterises the lower world as one of darkness and the upper as one of light, the heavens compounded of both, and says the Hebrew name for heaven joins fire and water.

quotes.text: This is the world of darkness; that the world of light; the heavens are compounded of light and darkness.
of a middle nature, the heavens are on that account called by the Hebrews asciamaim, as if composed of es and maim, that is, of the fire and water of which we spoke.

text: Pico contrasts the worlds: alternation of life and death below, eternal life and unchanging activity above, and in the heavens stability of life but change of activity and position.

quotes.text: Here there is an alternation of life and death; there, eternal life and unchanging activity; in the heavens, stability of life but change of activity and position.

text: Pico says the highest world is of the divine nature of mind, and that the third world is moved by the second and the second governed by the first.

quotes.text: bodies; that one of the divine nature of the mind; the heavens of body, but incorruptible, and of mind, but enslaved to body. The third is moved by the second; the second is governed by the first

text: Pico says Moses diagrammed the three worlds in the three parts of the tabernacle, the Holy of Holies with its winged cherubim being the angelic world.

quotes.text: these three worlds were clearly diagrammed by Moses in the construction of his wonderful tabernacle.
the more secret was distinguished with the name of Holy of Holies, the other simply as the Sanctuary, just as, although the celestial and angelic worlds are both holy
In the third part, the most sacred of all, were the winged cherubim.

text: Pico says that since the fall of Lucifer there is no stain or sin above the moon, and that the angelic world is held far more holy than the celestial.

quotes.text: because since the fall of Lucifer there neither is nor can be stain or sin above the moon, the angelic world is still held far more holy and divine than the celestial.

judged.justification: A location claim (no sin above the moon) that Pico states without discussion, relevant to the trial articles on where angels dwell.

text: Pico reads the rending of the temple veil at Christ's death as opening the way to the supercelestial world and communion with the angels.

quotes.text: Since the way to the supercelestial world, to commu- nion with the angels, was opened for us by the cross and blood of Christ, for that reason, at the moment of his death, the veil of the temple was rent asunder

text: Pico says the three worlds are one world because whatever is in any of them is contained in each of the others, and says his purpose almost wholly depends on this.

quotes.text: It should above all be observed, a fact on which our purpose almost wholly depends, that these three worlds are one world
because whatever is in any of the worlds is at the same time contained in each, and there is no one of them in which is not to be found whatever is in each of the others.

judged.justification: Pico himself names mutual containment as the hinge of the whole work; the fourfold and later expositions are derived from it.

text: Pico tentatively ascribes the doctrine of mutual containment to Anaxagoras, as expounded by the Pythagoreans and the Platonists.

quotes.text: If we have understood him rightly, I believe that this was the opinion of Anaxagoras, as expounded by the Pythagoreans and the Platonists.

hedge_words: If we have understood him rightly, I believe

open_questions.text: Pico names no text for the attribution to Anaxagoras beyond the Pythagoreans and Platonists who expound him.

text: Pico illustrates containment by heat: the element among us, the sun as fire in the sky, and the seraphic intellect as fire in the ultramundane region, differing in that the elemental fire burns, the celestial gives life and the supercelestial loves.

quotes.text: In our world there is the elemental quality of heat, in the heavens there is a heating power, and in angelic minds there is the idea of heat.
among us there is the fire which is an element; the sun is fire in the sky; in the ultramundane region the fire is the seraphic intellect.
The elemental fire burns; the celestial gives life, and the supercelestial loves.

judged.justification: Identifies the seraphic intellect with fire and love in the intelligible world by an explicit three-tier analogy.

text: Pico illustrates containment by water: the element in our world, the moon in the heavens, and the minds of the cherubim above the heavens; moisture quenches the heat of life below, feeds it in the heavens, and the supercelestial understands it.

quotes.text: There is water in our world; there is water in the heavens, the mover and mistress of ours, namely, the moon, the vestibule of the heavens
the heavens, the waters are the minds of the cherubim.
the elemental moisture quenches the heat of life; the celestial feeds it; the supercelestial understands it.

judged.justification: Ties the cherubic order to understanding by the same analogy.

text: Pico says that in the first world God, the primal unity, presides over nine orders of angels and, without moving, moves all toward himself.

quotes.text: In the first world, God, the primal unity, presides over nine orders of angels as if over as many spheres and, without moving, moves all toward himself.

judged.justification: States the nine orders and God as primal unity in the terms used later in the Third Exposition.

text: Pico says the empyrean heaven presides over nine heavenly spheres and is itself unmoving in imitation of God, and that the elemental world has nine spheres of corruptible forms after prime matter.

quotes.text: In the middle world, that is, the celestial, the empyrean heaven likewise presides like the commander of an army over nine heavenly spheres, each of which revolves with an unceasing motion; yet in imitation of God, it is itself unmoving.
There are also in the elemental world, after the prime matter which is its foundation, nine spheres of corruptible forms.

text: Pico says Scripture itself indicates mutual containment, in the Psalm that the heavens were made in understanding and in the text that angels are spirits and his ministers a flame of burning fire.

quotes.text: the mutual containment of the worlds is also indicated by the Holy Scriptures, both where it is written in the Psalms, "Who made the heavens in understanding," and where we read that the angels of God are spirits and his ministers a flame of burning fire.

text: Pico says the science of all allegorical interpretation flows from the mutual containment of the worlds, and that correct interpretation requires knowledge of the hidden alliances and affinities of nature.

quotes.text: this principle (in case anyone has not yet understood it) flows the science of all allegorical interpretation.
The early Fathers could not properly represent some things by the images of others unless trained, as I have said, in the hidden alliances and affinities of all nature.

judged.justification: Makes the cosmology the ground of the hermeneutics.

text: Pico says man is a fourth world containing what is in the rest, and that it is a school commonplace that man, the lesser world, includes reason, the angelic mind and the likeness of God.

quotes.text: There is, moreover, besides the three that we have mentioned, a fourth world in which are found all those things that are in the rest. This is man himself

It is a commonplace expression in the schools that man is a lesser world, in which are seen a body compounded from the elements, and a heavenly spirit, and the vegetative soul of plants, and the sense of brutes, and reason, and the angelic mind, and the likeness of God.

open_questions.text: Whether 'angelic mind' here names a faculty of the human soul distinct from 'reason' is not explained in this passage.

judged.justification: The angelic mind is listed as a component of man, as a school commonplace, not as a doctrine Pico argues here.

text: Pico says mutual containment yields a fourfold exposition: the text is read first of the angelic and invisible world alone, then the celestial, then the sublunary, then of the nature of man.

quotes.text: Hence there arises immediately a fourfold exposition of the whole Mosaic test, so that, in the first place, whatever is written there we interpret in relation to the angelic and invisible world, making no mention whatever of the others. In the second place, we interpret everything in relation to the celestial world; then in relation to this sublunary and corruptible one; and fourthly, in relation to the nature of man.

open_questions.text: The proem lists the angelic world first, but the contents give the elemental world first and the angelic third; the source states both orders and does not reconcile them.

judged.justification: The proem lists the angelic world first; the contents put the elemental world first and the angelic third.

text: Pico says the fifth exposition arises because the natures, though distinct, are linked, and the sixth shows fifteen ways in which one thing may be joined to another.

quotes.text: From this arises the necessity of a fifth exposition. It is added because, although these natures are distinct, there is no multiplicity which is not a unity
we are drawn in spite of ourselves to a sixth interpretation. In this we shall show that there are fifteen ways in which we can understand one thing as joined or related to another.

text: Pico says the seventh, sabbatical exposition treats the felicity of creatures and their return to God, and that the text hides an explicit prophecy of Christ, the Church and the calling of the gentiles.

quotes.text: it is fitting that after treating the orders of things proceeding from God and explaining their union and diversity and their bonds and habits, we should in a seventh, and as it were, sabbatical exposition, touch lightly on the felicity of creatures and their return to God

we shall disclose what in the present scripture Moses clearly hid about these, so that this explicit prophecy of the advent of Christ, of the increase of the Church, and of the calling of the gentiles, may be read plainly.

text: Pico says he will not pile up what philosophers and theologians have said about God, angels, matter and the heavens, as Isaac the Persian and Samuel Ophinides did, but will only show what the text means.

quotes.text: We shall not, however, imitate those who, having tried sometimes to explain the creation of the world, have heaped together whatever philosophers or theologians have anywhere said about God, the angels, matter, the heavens, and the whole of nature. Among the Hebrews, Isaac the Persian and Samuel Ophinides have particularly sinned in this.

judged.justification: States that the Heptaplus is meant to be brief on angels and other topics and to rely on the reader's prior learning.

text: Pico says the work is not meant to teach those who have not learned these matters elsewhere, but to let readers recognise in the words of the Prophet what they already know.

quotes.text: it is not the purpose of this work that any who have not learned these things elsewhere should learn them here for the first time, but that they may recognize in the words of the Prophet what they already know

text: Pico says the seven expositions are arranged in seven books of seven chapters each, and that the seventh chapter of each is turned to Christ as the Sabbath.

quotes.text: since the seven expositions are arranged in seven books and each book is divided into seven chapters, the whole corresponds to the seven days of creation.
we have taken care that every exposition of ours shall always in the seventh chapter be turned to Christ, who is the end of the law and is our Sabbath, our rest, and our felicity.

judged.justification: The seven are the seven expositions, each with seven chapters; nothing here describes seven interpretive layers within each exposition.

text: Pico says it is believable that the teaching of Moses about the worlds is arranged as God arranged them, so that the scripture of Moses is the exact image of the world.

quotes.text: it is believable that his teaching about the worlds is arranged just as God, the almighty artificer, arranged them in themselves, so that truly the scripture of Moses is the exact image of the world

text: Pico says the First Exposition treats the corruptible things below the moon, which the work of the first day includes, and starts from the natural philosophers' principles of matter, privation, efficient cause and form.

quotes.text: This is what is commonly said of corruptible things, all of which Moses so included in the work of the first day that the most excellent philosophers have said nothing about them any more certain or fitting.
The natural philosophers who treat of the nature of corruptible things hold this in general among their first principles: that there is a crude matter devoid of form

text: Pico says that the divine Platonists remind us natural agents are not primary causes but instruments of a divine art, so that the Platonists propose an instrumental and an ideal cause.

quotes.text: divine, remind us that although only natural agents seem to us to move, shape, and transform bodies, nevertheless they are by no means primary causes of the things which are made but rather instruments of a divine art which they obey and serve.
From this it comes that the Platonists themselves propose two causes, the instrumental and the ideal.

text: Pico reads heaven and earth in the first verse as the active and material causes, and says the Stoics called heaven the active cause and earth the material.

quotes.text: In the beginning, therefore, he sets up two causes, the active and the material, clearly that which is in act and that which is potentiality. He calls the former heaven and the latter earth
this interpretation of ours is confirmed by the authority of the Stoics, who called heaven the active cause and earth the material

text: Pico appeals to the ancient Simeon as testimony that the ancient Hebrews, like Albert and many Peripatetics, held the Hebrew word bou to signify the rudiments of form in matter.

quotes.text: Bou, on the other hand, by the force of the term, many explain as the rudiments and beginning of form.
Not only did Albert and many of the Peripatetics believe this, but also the ancient Hebrews, as we see clearly from the testimony of the ancient Simeon.

open_questions.text: Pico cites Simeon without a passage; an editorial note in the source points to the Zohar (I, 16a) at the parallel place, but the gate does not allow that note as a claim.

judged.justification: A rare place where the Zohar's author is invoked for a doctrinal point alongside the Peripatetics, in the elemental exposition.

text: Pico says that in the myth the poets ascribe the unitary rule of Saturn to the union of the intelligible world enfolding all within itself, after which the sensible world was divided among Jove (celestial), Pluto (subterranean) and Neptune (the region between moon and earth).

quotes.text: the poets concealed philosophy under veils of myth, when after the unitary rule of Saturn (that is, the union of the intelligible world enfolding all within

self) they divided the sensible world into three parts, ascribing the celestial region to Jove, the subterranean to Pluto, and this middle one between moon and earth, which we are now discussing, to Neptune, lord of the sea

judged.justification: Saturn is glossed as the union of the intelligible world, the angelic realm of the second proem, which bears on the Commento's Saturn.

text: Pico calls the Platonists ever the imitators of Hebrew learning.

quotes.text: Indeed, the Platonists, ever the imitators of Hebrew learning, call these forms generations rather than forms, because they can more truly be said to become than to be.

judged.justification: Shows the direction of dependence Pico assumes between Plato and Hebrew learning.

text: Pico says that as man is the perfection of all lower things, so Christ is the perfection of all men, and that man is the term at which the corruptible world halts.

quotes.text: Highest and foremost of all is man, having reached whom the nature of the corruptible world halts and sounds a retreat.
Just as man is the absolute perfection of all lower things, so Christ is the absolute perfection of all men.

text: Pico says a third explanation for Moses' figurative terms is that with them the same words, context and order suit all the worlds, so that the book of Moses excels all others in doctrine and is new and untouched.

quotes.text: Now we have occasion for a third explanation. If he had called matter and forms and qualities and active cause by their right names, they could have been of service in the discussion of the corruptible world, to be sure, but not in that of the others.

for symbolizing the secrets of all the worlds and of the whole of nature. It is in this respect that the book of Moses excels all other progeny of the human mind in doctrine, eloquence, and genius, and this is the new and hitherto untouched aspect which we have tried to present

judged.justification: Claims novelty for the reading in which one text serves all four worlds.

text: Pico says, on the authority of Dionysius and Thomas, that among angelic minds the highest is the one that understands with the fewest concepts what lower minds understand with many.

quotes.text: Similarly among angelic minds, according to the authority of Dionysius and St. Thomas, the glory of our theology, that is highest which by its intelligence understands with the fewest concepts and forms what lower minds understand with many and varied ones.

judged.justification: Pico cites Dionysius and Aquinas together as authorities on angelic knowledge, before the Third Exposition.

text: Pico says a tenth heaven, fixed and at rest, is believed to lie above the nine spheres.

quotes.text: Above the nine spheres of the heavens, that is, the seven planets and the eighth sphere, which is called that of the fixed stars, and the ninth sphere, which is apprehended by reason, not by sense, and which is first among the bodies that move, there is believed to be a tenth heaven, fixed, quiet, and at rest, which does not participate in motion.

text: Pico reports that Isaac the philosopher takes the tenth sphere to be what Ezekiel called the sapphire in the likeness of a throne, its immobility being signified by the likeness to a throne.

quotes.text: This Isaac takes the tenth sphere to be what Ezekiel designated as the sapphire in the likeness of a throne, since the color of the sapphire signifies the splendor of its light, the likeness to a throne its immobility.

judged.justification: A case where 'throne' names an unmoving heaven, not an angelic order.

text: Pico argues that the light of the visible heaven comes from the highest heavens, the tenth sphere being the unity of lights, and calls the tenth heaven the empyrean.

quotes.text: If light is to be traced back to one sphere as to its source, that is, to the tenth, which is then the unity of lights, then the ninth may be first to receive the light with the whole essence of its substance.
Therefore above the nine heavens let us suppose a tenth, which the theologians call the empyrean.

text: Pico says the empyrean governs the nine spheres beneath it as a general his army or a form its matter, and by exhibiting the image of unity completes the group of ten.

quotes.text: Therefore this sphere governs the nine coming beneath it in descending order, as a general his army or a form its matter; and exhibiting the image of unity, it completes the group of ten.

text: Pico reports a doubt whether the empyrean is corporeal and leaves the matter open, insisting only that the treasuries of light are there.

quotes.text: Some doubt whether its nature be corporeal or not rather incorporeal, since it is perhaps fitting for the unity of something, corresponding by an analogy of nature to the elemental number, not to be of the same sort as the thing.
let it remain unshaken that the treasuries of light are there and that from them as from a primal fountain whatever light is found and beheld in bodies is drawn off.

hedge_words: Some doubt whether its nature be corporeal or not rather incorporeal

open_questions.text: Pico leaves undecided whether the empyrean, which he compares to the unity presiding over the nine spheres, is corporeal.

text: Pico says the nine choirs of angels may be called gods because they participate in divinity, whereas God in the absolute sense is the indivisible Trinity presiding over them, as the empyrean presides over the nine orbits.

quotes.text: we may call the nine choirs of angels gods because they participate in divinity, from which comes the expression "God of gods," but when we say "God" in an absolute sense we do not understand one of them but the indivisible Trinity presiding over them, just as the empyrean heaven presides over the nine orbits subject to it.

judged.justification: Angels are called gods by participation, and God stands to the nine choirs as the empyrean to the nine spheres: the analogy of the second proem restated.

text: Pico reads the Spirit of the Lord that brooded over the waters as the empyrean, the closely adhering spiritual Olympus and seat of the Spirits of the Lord, warming the crystalline sphere with light.

quotes.text: Above this was borne or, as Hebrew wisdom has it and as Ephraim the SyrianS translates it, "brooded," the Spirit of the Lord; that is, the closely adhering spiritual Olympus, the seat of the Spirits of the Lord, warmed it with its life-giving light

judged.justification: Makes the empyrean the seat of spirits, while the Third Exposition reads the same words of the angelic intellect and of love.

text: Pico says that up to this point the Prophet has treated the heavens as luminous bodies and has said nothing of their intelligence or motive force, following the order of the Timaeus of body first and soul after.

quotes.text: Know, moreover, that thus far the heavens have been treated as luminous bodies and that nothing has been said by the Prophet of their intelligence or of their motive force, an order which the Timaeus also follows, first constructing the body and then adding the soul to the completed body.

text: Pico says that Moses, about to declare the heavens possessed of a rational soul, uses man as an allegory, meaning the rational soul, and that what is said of the soul of man is carried over to the soul of the heavens.

quotes.text: So much for the corporeal nature of the heavens. Now, about to declare them possessed of a rational soul, Moses uses man as an allegory, not the frail and earthly creature which we see, but the one by which, as Plotinus says

This is the rational soul itself, which in the Timaeus is formed of the same elements and in the same mixing bowl as the soul of the heavens, and not incongruously what is said of the soul of man is carried over to the soul of the heavens.

judged.justification: Pico takes the 'man' of the sixth day as the rational soul of the heavens in this exposition.

text: Pico says Scripture often represents all angelic and rational natures by man, as in the prophets for the good angels and for the evil demon, who does not differ from the good angels at all in nature.

quotes.text: The Holy Scriptures, in which all angelic and rational natures are often represented by man, agree with our interpretation. This usage is very common in the prophets for the good angels, and also for the evil demon, who does not differ from them at all in nature.

open_questions.text: Pico gives no argument here for the identity of nature of good and evil angels; the claim is asserted as a scriptural usage.

judged.justification: A flat statement that the evil demon does not differ in nature from the good angels, offered as an ordinary scriptural usage.

text: Pico says the heavenly souls do at once contemplation and the government of their bodies, and that the ancients, as in the Orphic hymns, named these two powers male and female.

quotes.text: Likewise it is not without mystery why God created that man male and female. It is the prerogative of the heavenly souls to perform simultaneously both the function of contemplation and that of governing their bodies, and the latter cannot hinder or be an obstacle to the former, nor the former to the latter.

It was commonly the practice of the ancients, as we observe in the Orphic hymns, to designate by the terms male and female these two powers in the same substance, one of which is engaged in contemplation while the other rules the body

text: Pico believes a mystery of the ancient wisdom of the Hebrews lies hidden here, the dogma that Jupiter and Mars are included by the sun and Venus and Mercury by the moon, and notes that the Hebrews themselves give no reason for it.

quotes.text: I believe that yet more deeply hidden here lies a mystery of the ancient wisdom of the Hebrews, among whose dogmas on the heavens this is important: that Jupiter and Mars are included by the sun, and Venus and Mercury by the moon.
although the Hebrews themselves offer no reason for the doctrine

judged.justification: An instance of Pico supplying a rationale for a Hebrew dogma that his sources leave unexplained.

text: Pico summarises what the Prophet has related of the celestial world: its divine body, the number of its spheres, its nature, properties, function, motive power, rational substance and intelligence.

quotes.text: These are the things related by the Prophet of the celestial world, that is, of its divine body, of the number of its spheres, of its nature, its properties, its function, and finally of its motive power, its rational substance, and its intelligence.

text: Pico invokes the Platonic notion that the Divine Artificer compounded our souls in the same mixing bowl and of the same elements as the celestial souls, and says man is a soul, an intelligence that transcends the boundaries of heaven and the passage of time.

quotes.text: we have not forgotten the Platonic notion we mentioned-not to speak of the theologians-that the Divine Artificer compounded our souls in the same mixing bowl and of the same elements as the celestial souls, let us take care not to wish ourselves the slaves of those whom nature wished to be our brothers.
As it is written in the Alcibiades, man is not this weak and earth-bound thing we see, but a soul, an intelligence, which transcends all the boundaries of heaven and all the passage of time.

judged.justification: Human souls are of the same stuff as the celestial souls and higher than the heavens, a premise for the Third Exposition's ranking of man against angels.

text: Pico cites the Chaldeans against exaggerating the influence of the stars and against seeking goods of body or fortune from the heavens, saying they will not give them.

quotes.text: The Chaldeans remind us of this, saying, "Do not exaggerate fate."
Let us not seek from the heavens goods of body or fortune, which they will not give, but from the Lord of heaven, the Lord of all good things

text: Pico says that much about the angelic and invisible nature was handed down by the ancient Hebrews and by Dionysius, and that his plan was to expound the words of Moses according to the teaching of both schools.

quotes.text: Since much about the angelic and invisible nature has been handed down by the ancient Hebrews and much also by Dionysius, it was my plan to expound the words of Moses according to the teaching of both schools.

judged.justification: Pico himself names two separate schools of angelology, Hebrew and Dionysian, and says he planned to use both; the Heptaplus's Third Exposition is therefore presented as only half the plan.

text: Pico says he decided to put off the Hebrew teaching because it is unfamiliar to the Latins and would require explaining nearly all the dogmas of the ancient Hebrew learning, which he will publish more fully elsewhere, examining how far they agree with Egyptian tradition, Plato and Catholic truth.

quotes.text: But since what is said by the Hebrews is unfamiliar to the Latins and could not easily be understood by our people unless, hatched from a twin egg, as they say, I explained nearly all of the dogmas of the ancient learning of the Hebrew people, I thought I ought to put it off until I have made these dogmas known to my countrymen by writing of them more fully elsewhere, examining how far they agree with the traditions of Egypt, the philosophy of Plato, and Catholic truth.

open_questions.text: Which work Pico means by writing 'more fully elsewhere' is not named in the passage.

judged.justification: Postpones the Hebrew angelology to another work; the Heptaplus's Third Exposition is deliberately Dionysian.

text: Pico says that where the Hebrews agree with 'us' he will hold them to their fathers' traditions, where they disagree he will attack them, and what is holy and true he will bear off from the synagogue to the legitimate Israelites.

quotes.text: If they agree with us anywhere, we shall order the Hebrews to stand by the ancient traditions of their fathers; if anywhere they disagree, then drawn up in Catholic legions we shall make an attack upon them.
whatever we find holy and true we shall bear off from the synagogue, as from a wrongful possessor, to ourselves, the legitimate Israelites.

judged.justification: States the concordist test Pico proposes to apply to Hebrew material.

text: Pico says that in the meantime he will tread in the footsteps of Dionysius, or rather Paul and Hierotheus, whom Dionysius followed, to bring light on the shadows of the law.

quotes.text: Meanwhile, treading in the footsteps of Dionysius, or rather Paul and Hierotheus, whom he followed, we shall try to the extent of our weakness to bring light upon those shadows of the law which the Spirit of God, the author of law, set up for his hiding place.

judged.justification: Pico places the Dionysian corpus in an apostolic line (Hierotheus, Paul, Dionysius) and chooses it as the guide of the Third Exposition.

text: Pico says every number is perfected by unity, and proposes to apply these notions to divine things after the Pythagorean custom.

quotes.text: Any number, after unity, is perfected and completed by unity. Unity alone, completely simple, perfected by itself, does not go beyond itself
Let us apply these notions to divine things, after the Pythagorean custom.

judged.justification: Pico himself labels the treatment of angels by number and unity Pythagorean; it ties the angelology to the doctrine of unity that later figures in the dispute over the One.

text: Pico says God alone is wholly simple and is being itself, and that other things are not being itself but exist by means of it.

quotes.text: God alone, who is derived from nothing and from whom all things are derived, is a wholly simple and individual essence.
We cannot understand any reason why he exists except that he is being itself. Other things are not being itself, but exist by means of it.

judged.justification: God is being itself and unity itself in this exposition, which bears on how Pico later states the convertibility of being and one.

text: Pico argues that an angel is not unity itself, since then he would be God, and so is left to be a number, a number in one respect and a multiplicity in another.

quotes.text: Therefore an angel is not unity itself, or else he would be God, or there would be many gods
It is left for an angel to be a number. But if it is, it is a number in one aspect and one multiplicity in another.

judged.justification: Angel as number (multiplicity in one respect, unity in another) is Pico's structure for angelic nature.

text: Pico says whatever is imperfect in an angel is to be ascribed to its multiplicity, as a creature, and whatever is perfect to its participation in unity, which it has from being associated with God.

quotes.text: Therefore, whatever is imperfect in an angel let us ascribe to the angel's multiplicity, which it has from being a number, that is, a creature; and whatever is perfect to its participation in unity, which it has from being associated with God.

text: Pico finds a double imperfection in an angel: that it is not being itself but an essence to which being comes by participation, and that it is not intelligence itself but only happens to understand, the second depending on the first.

quotes.text: In an angel we find a double imperfection: the one, that it is not being itself but only an essence to which being comes by participation, so that it may be; the other, that it is not intelligence itself but only happens to understand, since by its nature it is an intellect capable of understanding.
The second imperfection, however, depends on the first

judged.justification: States an essence-being composition and a distinction of intellect from its act in angels, in a passage that says nothing of matter.

text: Pico says God is the unity from which angels draw their being, life and all their perfection, and that their perfection comes by unity from above.

quotes.text: It remains for its perfection and completion to be produced by unity coming from above. God is the unity from which angels draw their being, their life, and all their perfection.

text: Pico reads the void and empty earth as the crude and unformed angelic essence which God created, and denies that only the formation of essence and not its creation is the work of the Artificer.

quotes.text: The first is that by which there exists the crude and unformed essence devoid of life and being, that is, the void and empty earth which God created. Do not believe, as many have believed, that only the formation of essence is the work of the Artificer, and not its creation also.

judged.justification: Applies the 'earth' of Genesis to angelic essence, as a created and initially unformed substrate of multiplicity.

text: Pico says that with the earth God created the heavens, meaning the actuality of that essence and the unity shared in multiplicity, that is, being itself.

quotes.text: At the same time as the earth He created the heavens, that is, the actuality of that essence and the unity which is shared in multiplicity, that is, being itself, so that the creation of heaven and earth is almost the same as that of a mutual embrace

text: Pico says an angel cannot fulfil understanding and contemplation unless surrounded by intelligible forms, and reads the deep as the angel's intellectual capacity, over which is the darkness until illuminated by spiritual concepts.

quotes.text: An angel, from what we have said, has perfectly realized his own nature and intellectual qualities. Nevertheless, he does not have a way to fulfill his functions of understanding and contemplation unless he is first surrounded by God with intelligible forms.

The deep is his intellectual capacity, penetrating and searching everything profound. Above this is the darkness, until it is illuminated by the rays of spiritual concepts by which he sees and contemplates everything.

text: Pico says the Spirit of the Lord is the spirit of love, that an angel is filled with spiritual light only by turning toward God, and that this turning is the motion of love, which follows understanding.

quotes.text: What will the Spirit of the Lord be other than the spirit of love? We cannot with propriety say that the spirit of knowledge is the Spirit of the Lord, because knowledge sometimes leads away from God. Love, however, always leads us to God.
This turning movement is not, and can not be, anything in the angelic nature but the motion of love.
was borne upon the deep, that is, upon the angelic intellect (for love follows understanding). Driven and excited by it, the mind of the angel turns toward God.

judged.justification: Makes love, not knowledge, the movement by which the angelic intellect is turned to God and lit; understanding precedes love.

text: Pico says light was made in the angel, the light of intelligible forms, and that intelligible species are united to angelic minds by eternal links and an indivisible bond, unlike the human intellect.

quotes.text: God said "Be light made," and light was made in the angel, the light of intelligible forms
let this reason be enough for us-that intelligible species are united to angelic minds by eternal links and an indivisible bond, not a vague and customary one as happens with the human intellect.

text: Pico reads the firmament set between the waters as signifying the three angelic hierarchies, the first and last being the waters above and below the heavens and the middle the firmament.

quotes.text: We read that the firmament was placed in the midst of the waters, by which are indicated to us the three hierarchies of angels (for thus we shall always call them, by the customary word). The first and last of these are designated by the waters, the former by those above the heavens, the latter by those which are under the heavens; the middle one dividing them is called the firmament.

judged.justification: Places the three Dionysian hierarchies in the Genesis text and gives them locations relative to the heavens.

text: Pico says, following Dionysius, that the highest hierarchy is given only to contemplation and praises God unceasingly, and that the middle rank is assigned to the work of the heavens.

quotes.text: All this, if we consider the nature and duties of the three hierarchies, could not be more in accord with the teaching of Dionysius. Since, as he writes, the highest hierarchy has leisure only for contemplation, it is properly symbolized by the waters that are placed above the heavens, that is, above all action in regard to worldly things, whether heavenly or earthly, and they praise God unceasingly with everlasting sound. Since the middle rank is assigned to the work of the heavens, it could not be more fittingly symbolized than by the firmament, that is, the sky.

judged.justification: Says the first hierarchy is purely contemplative and the second governs the heavens; the orders within them are not named here.

text: Pico says the last hierarchy, though above the heavens by nature, has charge of things under them and is divided into principalities, archangels and angels, whose activity concerns only what is under the moon.

quotes.text: The final hierarchy, although by nature it is above everybody and above the heavens, nevertheless has charge of things under the heavens. Since it is divided into principalities, archangels, and angels, all the activity of these is concerned only with what is under the moon; that of the principalities
with states and kings and princes, as we learn from Daniel, that of the archangels with mysteries and holy ceremonies; the angels are busy with private affairs and are assigned to men individually.

open_questions.text: The Third Exposition names the orders of only the third hierarchy; the assignment of the other six orders is not given in the passage.

judged.justification: Only the lowest hierarchy's three orders are named in this exposition; seraphim, cherubim and thrones are not mentioned in the exposition's scheme of hierarchies.

text: Pico says, following Paul, that the angels sent to carry out the duties of this world are all guardian spirits sent to minister to those who receive salvation, gathered into one place to look after the salvation of man alone.

quotes.text: What it may be for the waters under the heavens to be gathered together into one place would perhaps be doubtful if it were not explained to us by Paul, in whom we read that the angels sent to carry on the duties of this world are all guardian spirits sent to minister to those who receive the inheritance of salvation.
From this we can understand that these subcelestial waters, that is, the angelic armies, have been assembled into one place to look after the good and salvation of man alone.

text: Pico says the angels are said to be gathered in one place only as rivers flow to the ocean, since different angels preside over different corporeal and non-human things, as Platonists and Christian philosophers, Augustine, Gregory and Origen hold.

quotes.text: Scarcely otherwise should we understand the angels which have charge of sublunary things. Different ones preside over different corporeal and non-human things, since, just like the Platonists, our philosophers also have believed that God placed various spiritual substances in authority over the various things in this corruptible world.

Augustine also asserted, as Gregory later confirmed, that there is no visible thing among us over which an angelic power does not preside, and that all bodies are constantly ruled by a rational spirit of life.
Origen likewise, in his commentary on the book of Numbers, says that the world needs angels to preside over animals and their birth and also over the increase of bushes and plantings and other things

judged.justification: Angels as governors of particular bodies, with Augustine and Gregory as authority, bears on the location and function questions.

text: Pico reports the Damascene's opinion that the angel who sinned was one of the most contemptible kind, presiding over the terrestrial order, and says all the angels' care for lower things is subordinated to man's benefit.

quotes.text: The Damascene was also of this opinion, believing that the angel who sinned was one of those of the most contemptible kind who preside over the terrestrial order.
Just as all things below man are considered in relation to him, so all the care, toil, and zeal of the angels for these things is chiefly subordinated to his benefit

judged.justification: Records Pico's report of a view on the rank of the sinning angel.

text: Pico says the middle hierarchy administers heavenly matters, and that of the third hierarchy nothing more can be said beyond that it is above all active motion and given only to contemplation.

quotes.text: Now we are concerned with the middle one, to which is entrusted the administration of heavenly matters. We should not expect to treat similarly of the third, of which there is nothing to be said beyond what has been said, namely, that it is above the heavens, that is, above all active motion and above the administration of all worldly things, given only to contemplation.

open_questions.text: Pico calls the contemplative hierarchy the third here, although in chapter 3 he counts it the first; the source uses both orders without comment.

text: Pico says Moses' 'sun' and 'moon' are not the visible stars but the angelic powers which govern the sun and moon, and that these invisible angels illuminate an equally invisible earth, the substance of our souls.

quotes.text: In this place, however, let us not judge it extravagant nor foreign to the Holy Scriptures that Moses calls "sun" and "moon" not the stars which we see, but the angelic powers which govern the sun and moon.
let us understand not the stars, but the angels presiding over the stars, who, since they are invisible themselves, illuminate an earth which is also invisible, namely, the substance of our souls.

judged.justification: Angels are identified with the movers of the stars and the illuminators of human souls.

text: Pico says, citing Dionysius, that the three angelic activities of purification, illumination and perfection are distributed so that the lowest order purifies, the middle illuminates and the highest perfects with a fiery and life-giving dew.

quotes.text: since, as Dionysius says, there are three angelic activities, purification, illumination, and perfection, they are so distributed that the lowest order purifies, the highest perfects, and the middle one, which we are now discussing, illuminates.
the heavenly ones illuminate it when purified; the super celestial ones perfect it with a fiery and life-giving dew

judged.justification: Ties the orders to a triad of purgation, illumination, perfection as in the Oration, with the highest order 'fiery' (fire, seraph) and the lowest purgative.

text: Pico says the winged Seraphim of Isaiah and Ezekiel's birds and beasts, which the Hebrews take as spiritual substances, come to his aid, and that the ancient Hebrews all hold Moses here to intend the angelic host.

quotes.text: At this I would truly be in greater perplexity than anywhere else in this work if there did not come to my aid both Isaiah, in whom we read of the winged Seraphim, and Ezekiel, according to whom, if we believe the Hebrews, the birds and beasts symbolize spiritual substances.
the ancient Hebrews, all of whom hold that Moses here intended the angelic host, hasten to assist me

judged.justification: A place where the Hebrew reading is used positively for the angelic host, in an exposition otherwise on Dionysian lines.

text: Pico says the Prophet refutes the philosophers who admitted princely intellectual substances but denied that each is set over a multitude of lower rank, and that the leader of each of nine orders is to be imagined as a great sphere with its host as inhabitants.

quotes.text: Prophet refutes the error of the philosophers who believed that there are certain princely intellectual substances but denied that each of them is set over a numerous multitude of lower rank, like the commander of a legion, as the theologians say.

Since we know of nine orders of angels, and since each order has chosen its own leader by lot, let us fashion that leader and prince in our minds as a great sphere, and then the following army as the inhabitants and ornament of that sphere

open_questions.text: Pico does not name the philosophers who denied that each princely substance heads a multitude.

judged.justification: Nine orders, each with a leader over a multitude, imaged by spheres: a structural picture of the angelic world; the philosophers whose error is refuted are not named.

text: Pico says Moses mentions man in the angelic world not because man is an angel but because he is its end and terminus, placed between the incorporeal and the elementary, the end of one and the beginning of the other.

quotes.text: Finally Moses mentions man, not because man is an angel, but because he is the end and terminus of the angelic world, just as when discussing corruptible nature he presents man not as part of that nature, but as its beginning and head.

the discussion of man pertains to the three worlds, to that which is proper to him and to both extremes, the incorporeal and the elementary, between which he is placed so that he is the end of one and the beginning of the other.

judged.justification: Man is neither an angel nor part of the angelic hierarchy, but its terminus; contrast the second proem's 'angelic mind' as one of man's components.

text: Pico raises the objection that man is set over the beasts, birds and fish, which are read as angels, though the philosophers and the Prophet hold man lower than the angels, and answers that Christ as man enlightens and perfects the angels, if we believe Dionysius, and that all of us can be raised above the angels.

quotes.text: If these signify the angelic natures, how can what is written be true, that over them is set man, who, the philosophers know and the Prophet testifies, is lower than the angels?
human nature is so elevated that Christ as a man, so far as He is man, teaches, enlightens, and perfects the angels, if

we believe Dionysius, being made according to Paul much better than the angels, as He inherited a more excellent name than they; but also because all of us, to whom the power is given to become sons of God through the grace whose giver is Christ, can be raised to an honor above that of the angels.

judged.justification: Ranks Christ's humanity above the angels by appeal to Dionysius and Paul and says men can be raised above the angels through grace.

text: Pico says that above reason in man is intelligence, through which we share with the angels as we share through the senses with the brutes, so that we may say with John that our fellowship is with angels.

quotes.text: since we share no less with the angels than with the brutes, just as below reason there are the senses through which we have fellowship with the animals, so above reason is the intelligence through which we are able to say with John, "our fellowship is with angels."

judged.justification: Locates the human share in the angelic mind in an intelligence above reason.

text: Pico says a greater, even divine, intellect illuminates the human intellect, which some hold to be God and almost all the Greeks and Arabs and many Hebrews a mind nearer to man's, and that the Jewish philosophers and Alfarabi called this substance the Spirit of the Lord.

quotes.text: Here an important doctrine about the soul is revealed to us. A greater, even divine, intellect illuminates the

intellect in us, whether it be God (as some would have it) or a mind more nearly related to man's, as almost all the Greeks and Arabs and many of the Hebrews hold. This substance both the Jewish philosophers and Abunasar Alfarabi
called the Spirit of the Lord in explicit terms

judged.justification: Says the illuminating intellect is called the Spirit of the Lord by Jewish philosophers and Alfarabi, tying the Agent Intellect to the Genesis text, and reports a split between God and an intermediate mind.

text: Pico says Moses mentioned the bearing of the Spirit over the waters before the formation of man so that we would not think the Spirit present to our intellect only when it is joined to the body, an error he ascribes to Moses the Egyptian and Abubacher the Arab.

quotes.text: He did it lest we should by some chance believe this Spirit to be present to our intellect only when it is joined to the body. Moses the Egyptian, Abubacher the Arab,
and certain others falsely believed this.

judged.justification: Rejects a view of Maimonides and Abubacher on the conjunction of the separate intellect.

text: Pico says more recent philosophers would take the sun to be the active intellect and the moon the potential, but that since he is in a great controversy with them on this he will expound it otherwise for the time.

quotes.text: More recent philosophers would perhaps interpret the sun as the active intellect and the moon as the potential, but since we are in a great controversy with them on this point, we shall so expound it in the meantime

open_questions.text: Pico does not name the recent philosophers or state the controversy, and defers the point.

judged.justification: Pico says he is in a controversy over the identification of the active intellect and declines to use it here.

text: Pico says that although the author treats all worlds together everywhere, he assigned individual parts of his work to individual worlds in successive order, beginning with the first world, the angelic.

quotes.text: he assigned individual parts of his work peculiarly to the individual worlds in successive order. In order to show this, we shall begin to interpret the first part in relation to the first world, the angelic, and then the other parts in relation to the rest

judged.justification: Explains why the Fifth Exposition reads the sequence of the days as a sequence of worlds, angelic first.

text: Pico says the angelic nature is pure intellect and compares minds to eyes, which see by an inner light but need external light, so that the intellect needs forms and ideas as rays of invisible light.

quotes.text: To speak of the angelic nature, which is pure intellect, let us first imagine that minds are like eyes.

Intellects are eyes, intelligible truth is light, and the intellect, itself intelligible, has a kind of inner light by which it can see itself but not other things. It needs the forms and ideas of things, like rays of invisible light, for the intelligible truth to be clearly discerned.

text: Pico says that from the comparison of intellect to the eye arises the theory of those who consider intellect an unworthy name for God, since God is light itself and needs no step between intellect and the light.

quotes.text: From this arises the theory of those who consider "intellect" an unworthy appellation for God. If we compare the intellect with the eye, which does not see by itself but only with the help of light, then since God is light (for light is truth) and vision is the action in which the eye comes in contact with light, God does not need this step, since He is light itself

open_questions.text: Pico does not say whether he adopts the theory that 'intellect' is unworthy of God, nor whom he means by those who hold it.

judged.justification: Reports and appears to explain a theory that calls 'intellect' unworthy of God, bearing on the question of the One beyond intellect and being.

text: Pico says the common doctrine is that angels are composed of act and potency, that there is a troublesome dispute over what the act and the potency are and how they mingle, and that it is enough for him that the common opinion be somehow accepted.

quotes.text: The eye, that is, intellectual substance, is not wholly simple; otherwise it could not endure mingling with the oncoming light. From this comes the common doctrine that angels are
composed of act and potency, although there is a troublesome dispute as to what the act is, and what the potency, and what their manner of mingling
It is enough for us, as far as it concerns us here, for the common opinion to be somehow accepted.

open_questions.text: The passage does not say what the act and the potency are in an angel; the relation to the essence and being distinction of the Third Exposition is not stated.

judged.justification: Pico accepts the act-and-potency composition of angels as a common doctrine while refusing to settle the disputed terms.

text: Pico says Moses divides the substance of the angels on the first day into heaven and earth, the nature of act and the nature of potency, from which God made the angels.

quotes.text: All that we have said, Moses explains to us on the first day. He divides the substance of the angels into heaven and earth, the nature of act and the nature of potency.
God created heaven and earth, the nature of act and the nature of potency, from which he made the angels.

judged.justification: The Fifth Exposition reads heaven and earth as act and potency in angels, where the Third Exposition read them as being and essence.

text: Pico says the Spirit of the Lord borne upon the waters is called the Father of Lights by James, from which the light of intelligible forms rises upon the angelic minds.

quotes.text: Upon these waters was borne the Spirit of the Lord, the spirit which is called the Father of Lights by the apostle James, from which the light of intelligible forms soon rises upon them, that is, upon the angelic minds.

text: Pico says the heavens lie between the waters, meaning angelic and corruptible substances, in respect of their essence, and that there is one earth for the angels and another for the elements since the potency of the two differs.

quotes.text: Therefore the Prophet reveals to us his great knowledge of the nature of the heavens when he says that they are placed between the waters and the waters-that is, angelic and corruptible substances-in explanation not so much of their location as of their essence.
Just as there is one earth for the angels and another of the elements, since the potency of the two is different

text: Pico says that the astrologers draw support for their science of divining by the stars from the statement that the stars were made for signs, and that it has been sharply criticised by Christians such as Basil.

quotes.text: This point would require conversation with the astrologers, who, from Moses' statement that God placed the stars for signs, draw support for their science of divining by the stars and of foreknowing future events.
This science not only has been sharply criticized by Christians like Basil, who rightly called it a busy deceit

text: Pico says he puts off deeper questions to a projected work in which, reconciling Aristotle to Plato, he has undertaken to discuss and examine the whole of philosophy.

quotes.text: Therefore we put them off for the projected work in which, reconciling Aristotle to Plato, we have undertaken to discuss and examine the whole of philosophy to the best of our ability.

judged.justification: Sets the concordist project of reconciling Plato and Aristotle as the planned work into which philosophical detail is deferred.

text: Pico says that his friend Marsilio Ficino will soon give Plotinus to be read in Latin with ample comments, and cites Plotinus for the view that all life arises from a divine origin.

quotes.text: or whether all life arises rather from a divine origin, as asserted by Plotinus
whom, to the public advantage, our friend Marsilio Ficino will soon give us to read in Latin, illuminated by ample comments.

bears_on.note: Pico names Ficino 'our friend' and looks forward to his Latin Plotinus with commentary.
Pico cites Plotinus for a divine origin of life and awaits Ficino's translation.

judged.justification: Pico calls Ficino his friend and anticipates his Latin Plotinus in the Heptaplus.

text: Pico says man is not so much a fourth world as the bond and union of the three already described.

quotes.text: Thus far we have dealt with three worlds: the supercelestial, the celestial, and the sublunary. Now we must deal with man, of whom it is written, "Let us make man to our image." Man is not so much a fourth world, like some new creature, as he is the bond and union of the three already described.

open_questions.text: The second proem calls man 'a fourth world'; the Fifth Exposition says he is 'not so much a fourth world' as their bond; the source states both without reconciling them.

judged.justification: Qualifies the second proem's description of man as a fourth world.

text: Pico says that reason and mind are like God, intelligent, invisible and incorporeal, that man is like God especially in that part of the soul which displays the image of the Trinity, and that the angels, in whom these are stronger and less mixed, have more likeness and affinity with the divine nature.

quotes.text: and revert to the nature of reason and mind, which like God is intelligent, invisible, and incorporeal, we shall prove that man is like God, especially in that part of his soul which displays the image of the Trinity. But let us recognize that as in the angels these same things are much stronger and less mixed with the opposite nature than in us, the angels have more likeness and affinity with the divine nature.

text: Pico says the substance of man encompasses by its very essence the substances of all natures, and that not only angels but any intelligent creature includes all things in itself in some degree when, filled with their forms, it knows them.

quotes.text: What can it be but the substance of man which (as some Greek commentators intimate) encompasses by its very essence the substances of all natures and the fullness of the whole universe? I say by its very essence, moreover, because not only the angels, but any intelligent creatures whatever include all things in themselves in some degree when, filled with their forms and reasons, they know them.

judged.justification: Man's containing of all natures is put as distinct from the angelic containing of things by knowing them.

text: Pico says God contains all things in himself as their origin and man contains them as their center, so that in God all things are of better stamp than in themselves whereas in man inferior things are of nobler mark and the superior degenerate.

quotes.text: The difference between God and man is that God contains all things in Himself as their origin, and man contains all things in himself as their center. Hence in God all things are of better stamp than in themselves, whereas in man inferior things are of nobler mark and the superior are degenerate.

judged.justification: Repeats the better-stamp / degenerate contrast of the second proem for the case of man.

text: Pico says that man has the sense of the brutes, a soul powerful in heavenly reason and participation in the angelic mind, the simultaneous possession of all these natures being truly divine.

quotes.text: There is the sense of the brutes, inner and outer; there is the soul, powerful in its heavenly reason; there is participation in the angelic mind. There is the truly divine, simultaneous possession of all these natures flowing together into one, so that we may exclaim with Mercury

open_questions.text: The text does not say whether 'participation in the angelic mind' means sharing an intellect or a capacity for angelic knowing.

judged.justification: Man participates in the angelic mind; this is the phrase Pico's later writing might be compared with.

text: Pico says the heavens labor for man and the angelic minds look after his salvation and beatitude, if what Paul writes is true that all ministering spirits are sent to those destined for salvation.

quotes.text: the heavens labor for it, and the angelic minds look after its salvation and beatitude, if what Paul writes is true, that all ministering spirits are sent to minister to those who are destined for salvation as their inheritance

hedge_words: if what Paul writes is true

text: Pico says there are hangmen and lictors in the commonwealth of God, evil demons sentenced to this basest of professions as punishment for their ancient sins.

quotes.text: There are hangmen and lictors in this commonwealth of God, evil demons sentenced to this basest of professions as punishment for their ancient sins.

judged.justification: Assigns fallen angels a role as executioners in the cosmic commonwealth.

text: Pico says that, because all things are included in man, the gospel saying is that all the angels rejoice in gladness when a sinner repents.

quotes.text: Just as every creature hates and abhors the sins of man, so his upright life and behavior is dear and pleasing to all. All the things which are included in man and connected with him by so close a bond cannot be excluded from participation in his good and evil.
Hence comes the saying in the gospel, "If a sinner has repented, all the angels rejoice in gladness,"

text: Pico says that the unity seen in creatures is of three modes: each thing one to itself, one creature united to another, and the whole universe one with its Maker, and that each is derived from that One which is at once first one and three and one.

quotes.text: the fact that the unity which we see in creatures is of three different modes. First, there is that unity in things whereby each is one to itself, remains the same as itself, and is in harmony with itself. Secondly, there is that through which one creature is united to another and through which all parts of the world are ultimately one world. The third and most important of all is that whereby the whole universe is one with its Maker, as an army is with its leader.

This threefold unity is present in each thing through its own single and simple unity derived from that One which is both the first one and at the same time three and one, the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit.

judged.justification: Identifies the One with the Trinity in the Heptaplus's account of unity, relevant to the later exchange about the One and Being.

text: Pico says the power of the Father distributes unity to all, the wisdom of the Son sets all in order and unites them, and the love of the Spirit turns everything toward God and attaches the whole work to its Maker.

quotes.text: The power of the Father, creating everything, distributes his own unity to all; the wisdom of the Son, setting all in order, unites them and ties them together; and the love of the Spirit, turning everything toward God, attaches the whole work to its Maker by the bond of charity.

text: Pico says that the threefold unity in creatures, as a sign of the Trinity, has so far as he knows not been brought up by anyone before.

quotes.text: There are many signs of the Holy Trinity in the creation. We shall here take up only one of these, which as far as I know has not hitherto been brought up by anyone

text: Pico says that after running through all the doctrines of the philosophers he found not more than fifteen kinds of affinity between things and that he saw them all pointed out in Moses.

quotes.text: When I considered, before approaching the interpretation of the words, how many ways exist or can be thought of in which things may find an affinity or a bond with each other, and when I ran through all the doctrines of the philosophers on which I have sweated since boyhood, not more than fifteen kinds suggested themselves.
These, on turning to Moses, I saw so clearly and appropriately pointed out that I do not believe one can be better instructed in them anywhere else.

text: Pico says the Spirit of God is joined to bodies only as art in the mind of an architect is joined to mortar, wood and stone, being a spiritual nature wholly disjoined from traffic with the body, and that in us heaven is the soul and the Spirit of God the intellect.

quotes.text: The creative wisdom of the Lord, and the spiritual nature wholly disjoined from traffic with the body, are understood to be joined to bodies only as art, which is in the mind of the architect, is joined to mortar, wood, and stone.
Heaven is the soul, the source of that light, and the Spirit of God
is the intellect, the light of the divine countenance.

judged.justification: Says the Spirit of God, read in us as the intellect, is joined to bodies as an art to its matter, the language used of a separate intellect.

text: Pico says the mean is not of the same essence as the extremes but is somehow compounded from them so that it may communicate with both, and that Moses shows this by placing the firmament between the waters.

quotes.text: But the mean is not of the same essence as the extremes, but, somehow compounded from them, it differs from both so that it may communicate with both, Moses indicates this to us when he places the firmament between the waters, dividing the waters above the heavens from the waters below the heavens.

text: Pico says that our happiness is that whatever share of intellectual light is in us must be joined some day to the first intellect and the first mind of all, which is the fullness and totality of all understanding.

quotes.text: just as it is plainly the final happiness of drops of water to reach the ocean, which is the fullness of the waters; so for our happiness, whatever share of intellectual light is in us must be joined some day to the first intellect and the first mind of all, which is the fullness and totality of all understanding.

judged.justification: States that the human intellect is to be joined to the first intellect.

text: Pico says the extremes can be joined only through the mean, which must already have united them in itself, and that this mean is Christ, through whom alone the flesh can ascend to the Word.

quotes.text: Let us therefore keep it in mind that the coupling of the extremes can be brought about only through that nature which, as the mean between them embracing both, unites them suitably with each other, because it has already united them together in itself through the peculiarity of its own nature.
then it is through Christ alone that the flesh can ascend to the Word

text: Pico says the end of all things is the same as their beginning, one God, and that the Pythagoreans called him One and Good, One because he is the beginning as unity is the beginning of numbers, and Good because he is the end and absolute felicity.

quotes.text: Felicity I define as the return of each thing to its beginning.

Therefore the end of all things is the same as the beginning of all: one God, omnipotent and blessed, the best of all things which can exist or be thought of; hence the two appellations used by the Pythagoreans, One and Good. He is called one since He is the beginning of all things, just as unity is the beginning of all numbers, and good since He is the end, rest, and absolute felicity of all things.

bears_on.note: The pairing of One and Good as names of God is relevant to the later dispute over the priority of the One and Being, but the passage names no opponent.

judged.justification: Ties One to beginning and Good to end, and attributes the pair to the Pythagoreans, in the work's closing account of felicity.

text: Pico says the angelic mind is highest among creatures in natural felicity because of the nobility of its substance and its closeness to its end, and that in this felicity neither plants, animals, men nor angels attain God in himself but only in themselves.

quotes.text: Highest among creatures is the angelic mind, because of the nobility of its substance and its attainment of its end, in which it participates in the highest degree because it is close to it and joined to it.
But indeed, as we said above, through this felicity neither plants nor animals nor men nor angels attain God, who is the highest good, in God Himself, but only in themselves.

text: Pico says the philosophers who spoke only of natural felicity ascribe to the angels no knowledge of God beyond that by which the angels know themselves, so that they understand God only as his nature is manifest in their own substance.

quotes.text: In fact, even to the angels, whom they call minds and intellects, and whose supreme perfection they acknowledge because the angels understand God, they ascribe no further knowledge of God than that by which angels know themselves, so that the angels understand God only so far as His nature is made manifest in their own substance.

judged.justification: Pico reports a limit on angelic knowledge of God that he then says only grace overcomes.

text: Pico says that Avicenna, Averroes, Abu Bakr, Alexander and the Platonists seem to allow somewhat more, founding reason on the active intellect or on some greater one related to us, but lead man neither to his beginning nor to his end, and that he neither rejects nor despises their arguments as speaking of natural felicity.

quotes.text: Avicenna, Averroes, Abu Bakr, Alexander, and the Platonists seem to allow somewhat more, basing our reason, as on its proper end, on the active intellect or on some greater one which is nevertheless related to us; but they lead man neither to his beginning nor to his end. I neither reject nor despise their arguments and opinions, if they are taken as speaking only of natural felicity.

judged.justification: Pico grades the active-intellect theories as adequate only to natural felicity.

text: Pico says the angels can be raised to the true felicity, the contemplation of the face of God, but cannot ascend to it, Lucifer having sinned in saying he would ascend, and that men can be drawn but not go, the drawing power being called grace, which makes men and angels pleasing to God.

quotes.text: The true and perfect felicity, however, carries us back to the contemplation of the face of God, which is the whole of the good, as He himself said, and leads us to perfect union with the beginning from which we sprang. The angels can be raised to this, but they cannot ascend to it; thus Lucifer sinned in saying "I will ascend into heaven."
These rays, this divine power, this influence, we call grace, since it makes men and angels pleasing to God.

judged.justification: Puts angels, as well as men, in need of grace to reach the beatific vision and links the sin of Lucifer to trying to ascend by one's own power.

text: Pico says that true felicity is to be one spirit with God, possessing God in God and not in ourselves, and that from every imperfection of multiplicity we are brought back to unity by an indissoluble bond with him who is himself the One.

quotes.text: This is the true felicity, to be one spirit with God, so that we possess God in God, not in ourselves, knowing him just as we are known.
this is the wisdom which the wise men of this world do not know, that from every imperfection of multiplicity we are brought back to unity by an indissoluble bond with him who is himself the One.

judged.justification: Restates the angel-as-number teaching of the Third Exposition for man: return from multiplicity to unity, and calls God 'the One'.

text: Pico says the two natures capable of the highest felicity are the angelic, called heaven, and the human, called earth, and that Moses says no more of heaven since he is writing the law for men and not for angels.

quotes.text: As we have shown, two natures are capable of this highest felicity, the angelic and the human. The former is called heaven,
the latter earth, since the angels live in heaven and we on earth. Of heaven there is no reason for Moses to say more, since he is writing the law for men, not for angels.

open_questions.text: The Seventh Exposition again assigns 'heaven' and 'earth' to new referents (angels and men); the source reads the same words differently in each exposition, as the second proem announces.

judged.justification: Here 'heaven' means the angelic nature and 'earth' the human, as opposed to the readings of the Third and Fifth Expositions.

text: Pico says the Word of God confirmed the law given to Moses by the angel, and that the gentiles worship the demons dwelling in the murky air.

quotes.text: Therefore the Word of God confirmed the law given to Moses by the angel, which hitherto, more than the greater light, distinguished the Israelites from the gentiles
the gentiles are the waters under the heavens: they worship and adore the demons dwelling in the murky air, which is the region above the waters

judged.justification: Places demons in the air and says an angel gave the law to Moses.
