text: Pico says his interpretation will furnish weapons against the stony hearts of the Hebrews drawn from their own arsenals, and that it is among the doctrines of ancient Hebrew learning that the six days denote the six thousand years of the world, a view confirmed by Moses of Gerona and mentioned by Jerome.

quotes.text: Against the stony hearts of the Hebrews it will furnish you with powerful weapons drawn from their own arsenals.
It is among the doctrines of ancient Hebrew learning that the six days of Genesis denote the six thousand years of the world
Among the more recent authors this opinion is also confirmed by Moses of Gerona, a theologian of foremost fame among the Hebrews. St. Jerome also mentions it

judged.justification: Shows Pico using Hebrew sources polemically, in his own words as weapons against the Hebrews.

text: Pico says that the oracles of Elijah circulate among the Hebrews as well-understood traditions and that he will give the testimony of the Talmudists from the tractate Aboda Zara, which acknowledge that the time predicted by Elijah for the Messiah has passed.

quotes.text: There circulate among them as well-understood popular traditions the oracles of Elijah, which say freely and without any symbolism or veil that the Messiah will come in the fourth millennium of the world.
But the Hebrews will say, "Granted that Jesus came at this time."
These words are in the part which is entitled Aboda Zara

I shall offer the testimony of the very Talmudists with whom our controversy lies, who not only mention these oracles but, with the truth itself compelling them, acknowledge that the time predicted by Elijah for the coming of the Messiah has passed.

text: Pico says that, as Jonathan the Chaldean attests, evil demons are often represented in the Holy Scriptures by animals that live in the waters.

quotes.text: because, as Jonathan the Chaldean attests, evil demons are often represented in the Holy Scriptures by animals which live in the waters.

text: Pico says that having completed the sevenfold interpretation he will treat the first phrase last, that he will not discuss the Son as beginning nor prove that the ancient Hebrews thought as he does, which he will do elsewhere, and that he intends through another system of interpretation to give a taste of Mosaic profundity.

quotes.text: Now we have come to the end of our work, having gone through the sevenfold interpretation of the entire text.

I am not here going to discuss the Son of God, who is the beginning through which all things were made (for he is the wisdom of the Father), nor shall I prove here that the ancient Hebrews thought as we do, for I shall do this elsewhere. But I intend, through another system of interpretation, to give my readers a taste of Mosaic profundity.

judged.justification: Calls the sevenfold interpretation complete and treats the first phrase as a separate, additional method.

text: Pico says it is the firm opinion of all the ancients that the five books of the Mosaic law contain all knowledge, hidden in the very letters of the phrases, and that by the rules the Hebrews hand down the letters of a passage may be joined into sayings.

quotes.text: It is the firm opinion of all the ancients, unanimously asserted as beyond doubt, that the five books of the Mosaic law contain the entire knowledge of all arts and wisdom both divine and human. This knowledge is hidden and concealed, however, in the very letters of which the phrases of the law are composed.
If we open up the words and take the same letters separately and, according to the rules which the Hebrews hand down, join them together properly into the sayings that can be made up of them

judged.justification: Gives Pico's own account of the letter-permutation method and its authority.

text: Pico says he cannot prove what he claims about the method, having neither tested it nor confidence of being able to, but that he does not deny or despise it, partly because it has mighty supporters.

quotes.text: We cannot learn dogmas and doctrines here; we can only recognize them. I cannot prove or demonstrate what I claim, since I neither have made a test of it nor have confidence of being
but I do not deny or despise this theory, partly because it has mighty supporters, and partly because even greater things can easily be believed of Moses

hedge_words: I cannot prove or demonstrate what I claim

open_questions.text: Pico names no supporters of the permutation method in this passage.

judged.justification: Pico himself states the limits of his warrant for the Hebrew permutation method.

text: Pico says that on applying the rules of the ancients to the first phrase he found the whole plan of the creation of the world and of all things in it disclosed in that one phrase.

quotes.text: Applying the rules of the ancients to the first phrase of the work, which is read Beresit by the Hebrews and "In the beginning" by us, I wanted to see whether I too could bring to light something worth knowing.

Beyond my hope and expectation I found what I myself did not believe as I found it, and what others will not believe easily: the whole plan of the creation of the world and of all things in it disclosed and explained in that one phrase.

text: Pico gives as the resulting reading that the Father, in the Son and through the Son, the beginning and end or rest, created the head, the fire and the foundation of the great man with a good pact.

quotes.text: If we fit the whole passage together following this order, it will read like this: "The father, in the Son and through the Son, the beginning and end or rest, created the head, the fire, and the foundation of the great man with a good pact."

judged.justification: The Hebrew phrase is resolved into a Trinitarian statement and a description of the great man.

text: Pico says the world is the great man and that Moses represents the intellectual, heavenly and corruptible worlds by the head, the breast and the lower part, the angelic world being the fountain of knowledge because that nature was made for understanding.

quotes.text: In the first place, therefore, it should be noticed that the world is what Moses calls "the great man." For if man is a little world, then certainly the world is a great man.

Likewise in the world the highest part, which is the angelic or intellectual world, is the fountain of knowledge, because that nature was made for understanding. The middle part, which is the sky, is the principle of life, motion, and heat, in which the sun rules as the heart does in the breast.

judged.justification: Maps the three worlds onto head, breast and lower body, so that the angelic world is the intellect of the great man.

text: Pico says Moses named the highest part the head, the second fire because many refer to the sky by that name, and the third the foundation, and that the pact is good because it is directed toward God, the good itself, so that the world is one with its Maker.

quotes.text: Moses designated the first by its proper name, the head. The second, however, he called fire, because by this name many refer to the sky, and because in us this part is the principle of heat. The third he called the foundation

This pact is good, therefore, because it is directed and oriented toward God, who is the good itself, so that just as within itself the whole world is one, so also it is, in the end, one with its Maker.

text: Pico says the reading explains the whole plan, relationship and felicity of the four worlds he has discussed.

quotes.text: It is not easy for everyone to see immediately that here is explained the whole plan, relationship, and felicity, which we treated last of all, of the four worlds that we have discussed.
